entities.summary:
Alexander Hegius von Heek (c. 1430, Heek, Münster – 1498-12-16, Deventer) stands as a pivotal figure in the Northern Renaissance, serving as a transitional intellectual who bridged the spiritual fervor of the *Devotio Moderna* with the burgeoning classical humanism of the late 15th century. As rector of the Hieronymus School in Deventer from 1483 until his death, Hegius transformed this institution into one of Europe's most influential educational centers, directly shaping a generation of scholars, including the young Erasmus of Rotterdam. His innovative curriculum, emphasizing rigorous Latin and the then-uncommon study of Greek, laid critical groundwork for the broader humanist movement in the Low Countries and beyond, challenging scholastic traditions with a renewed focus on original classical texts.

Hegius's educational reforms at Deventer were profound and practical. He shifted the pedagogical focus away from rote memorization of medieval commentaries towards a direct engagement with classical authors such as Cicero, Virgil, and Horace, alongside Christian humanists like Lactantius. Crucially, Hegius introduced Greek language instruction, a rarity in Northern European schools before the 16th century, thereby opening up direct access to the New Testament and patristic writings in their original forms. His own scholarly output, though modest in publication (including *Carmina* and *Dialogi*), primarily manifested through his teaching and the intellectual environment he cultivated.
